passage:
"Two hundred and forty comments," Nirmala said, holding out her phone. "They're calling me a fraud. I have to reply."

"So reply," said her brother Hrithik, tearing his chapati at the dinner table. "Set them straight."

"If I write now, I'll be shaking and I'll say something I can't take back. I know myself."

"They'll think you're hiding."

"Let them. Tomorrow I'll be calmer, and then I can decide whether any of it deserves an answer."

Mummy looked up from the sink. "Put it in the drawer, beta. Eat."

Nirmala slid the phone under a cushion and took a chapati. Her hands were still trembling, but she had chosen not to answer tonight.

qa.q: How many comments did Nirmala see?
What is Nirmala afraid of if she replies straight away?
qa.a: Nirmala fears that she will be shaking and say something she cannot take back, so her worry is about acting in the heat of the moment.

qa.q: What could Nirmala do tomorrow before deciding whether to reply, and why?
qa.a: Nirmala could read a few comments calmly and ask a trusted person what they think, because a cooler head can tell which comments need a response.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see Nirmala's decision to wait?
qa.a: Hrithik thinks silence looks like hiding, so he may worry for her, though he would see she is calmer by tomorrow.

grounding: After a badly received post, the student sees hostile comments and waits a day, letting emotion drop and avoiding a reply that fuels the storm.

subtype: Approach: pause and avoid replying in the heat of the moment [Thinking]
passage:
I posted a short video about how my college's fest threw away trays of food every night. I thought I was being honest. By morning it had been shared by pages I'd never heard of, and there were over five hundred comments calling me ungrateful, attention-seeking, a liar.
My thumbs were already typing. I had a whole reply ready, full of capital letters. Charu, my roommate, just said, "Read it again tomorrow. If you still want to post it then, post it."
I sat on the bed and argued with myself. Right now I'm angry. Anything I write now, they'll screenshot. Tomorrow I'll still be right, if I'm right. So I saved the draft and put the phone in Charu's cupboard.
The next day I read the draft and cringed. I deleted it. The comments slowed on their own by evening. I'm Salma, and waiting was the smartest thing I did that week.

qa.q: How many comments were there by morning?
qa.a: There were over five hundred comments.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling while the reply was being typed?
qa.a: Salma was angry and hurt, typing a reply full of capital letters after being called ungrateful and a liar.

qa.q: What else could Salma have done during that waiting day?
qa.a: Salma could have talked it through with Charu or another trusted person, which would help sort the fair comments from the cruel ones.

qa.q: How might Charu have felt holding the phone in the cupboard?
qa.a: Charu may have felt protective and a bit anxious, wanting to help without taking over Salma's choice about replying.

grounding: Shows a student in a pile-on reasoning that a reply written in anger will feed the storm and choosing to wait a day before answering.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Wednesday. Written by Nitin, student wellbeing office.
Trisha came in at eleven, phone gripped face down. A reel she made about her hostel mess had been picked up by bigger accounts. She said there were hundreds of comments, many insulting her, and she wanted to "reply to all of them right now."
I asked what she thought a reply would do. She was quiet, then answered herself: "If I reply now I'll sound as angry as they are. They'll quote me. It'll get bigger." After a moment she said, "Tomorrow I'll know what I actually want to say."
She decided to log out until the next afternoon. We checked the comments together for any threats; there were none, only insults. She asked to come back tomorrow.
Next step: meeting booked for Thursday at three. I also gave her the evening helpline number in case the night felt heavy.

qa.q: What time did Trisha come to the wellbeing office?
What does Trisha's phone gripped face down suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt overwhelmed and tense, wanting the comments out of sight but not able to let go of the phone.

qa.q: What else could Trisha do while she waits?
qa.a: She could ask a trusted friend to watch the comments for threats, so she can stay logged out without worrying about missing something serious.

qa.q: How does Trisha's decision look to the counsellor?
qa.a: The counsellor sees a student who worked out for herself why replying now would make things worse, and supports that choice with a meeting and a helpline number.

grounding: Shows a student in an online pile-on reasoning aloud that an angry reply would fuel it and choosing to wait until the next day.
